raw_case_text:
An 11-year-old boy presented with a one-month history of proximal muscle weakness and a typical heliotrope rash, and was admitted to our hospital in July, 2022. His CMAS score was 12. Serum CK was elevated (4,718 U/L, reference range: 0-164 U/L). Electromyography indicated myogenic damage. Muscle biopsy showed typical perifascicular atrophy, inflammatory cells primarily distributed around the muscle fascicles, endomysium, and small blood vessels, and extensive positive staining of MHC I on the muscle membrane. MSA analysis confirmed the presence of anti-NXP2 antibody and anti-Ro-52 antibody. Anti-NXP2 antibody IgG level was 115.42 RU/ml, with ANA 1:320 (+). He was diagnosed with definite JDM according to 2017 EULAR/ACR criteria with a total aggregate score 14.9 > 8.7. Considering the critical condition of the patient, he was initiated on IVIG at a dose of 2 g/kg and IVMP at 500 mg/day for three days, followed by oral prednisone at 2 mg/kg/day. A dose of IVCY at 500 mg was also administered.
After treatment, muscle weakness persisted, and the patient gradually developed dysphagia. Two weeks after treatment, he suddenly experienced tonic-clonic seizures and remained in a coma between seizures, indicating status epilepticus. Sedative medications and assisted ventilation via endotracheal intubation were administered, and he was promptly admitted to the PICU. Physical examination revealed significant skin and periorbital edema (Figure 4A). Blood pressure was 126/81 mmHg. Cardiac and pulmonary physical examination showed no abnormalities. There were no enlarged lymph nodes or hepatosplenomegaly. Positive Babinski sign was observed bilaterally, while other pathological signs were negative. Laboratory examinations revealed elevated levels of AST (269 U/L), ALT (76 U/L), LDH (1,200 U/L), and CK (4,784 U/L). White blood cell count was 17.15 x 109 /L, with 91.4% neutrophils. Hemoglobin level was 137 g/L, and platelet count decreased to 39 x 109 /L. C-reactive protein level was within normal range. Serum ferritin was significantly elevated (>2,000 ng/ml), indicating hyperferritinemia. Triglyceride was 2.56 mmol/L. Serum electrolytes were in the normal range. There were no coagulation disorders. NXP2 antibody titer IgG was higher than initial admission: 139.76 RU/ml. Echocardiography showed normal cardiac function. Chest CT indicated bilateral lung infiltrates and partial consolidation. Cerebral CT showed blurred gray-white matter differentiation, and contrast-enhanced cerebral MRI (Figure 5A) revealed abnormal signals in the left parieto-occipital lobe and thalamus. Cerebral MRA and MRV were negative. EEG showed diffuse background slow waves (2-5 Hz low-to-moderate amplitude slow waves). Spinal fluid studies revealed normal cell counts and glucose level, with a slight increase in protein concentration (64 mg/dl, reference range: 15-45 mg/dl), and no evidence of bacteria or viruses.
After a thorough examination and analysis, considering the significant skin and periorbital edema, muscle weakness, significantly elevated muscle enzymes, and an increasing trend in NXP2 antibody titer IgG, we concluded that the patient was in the active stage of JDM, and seizures were attributed to CNS involvement. Considering the patient's worsening condition despite conventional treatment, we discussed his case and decided to initiate therapeutic PEs. As shown in Figure 6, four PEs were performed, including two sessions of double filtration plasmapheresis. IVMP (1.6 mg/kg/day) and maintenance IVIG (2 g/kg/month) was continued. In addition, pneumocystis jirovecii was detected in the metagenome next-generation sequencing analysis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid on PICU hospitalization day 6, so antifungal treatments were administered. Despite intensive PE treatment, his condition deteriorated further, and CK levels increased to 16,219 U/L. Two additional courses of IVMP therapy (500 mg/day for three days), over a two-week interval, were administered. Considering that the patient presented with hyperferritinemia and thrombocytopenia, macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) could not be ruled out, despite the absence of fever. Therefore, oral administration of tacrolimus (i.e., FK506) was initiated. Subsequently, a bone marrow examination revealed the presence of macrophages. In addition, tracheostomy was performed because prolonged intubation was needed.
After the treatments, the patient's seizures ceased, muscle strength improved, swallowing and respiratory functions recovered, and muscle enzyme levels decreased to 41 U/L. The patient was successfully weaned off the ventilator. On hospitalization day 58, EEG showed a baseline electrical activity of 9-10 Hz alpha waves with some theta and delta waves. Cerebral MRI on hospitalization day 28 (Figure 5B) indicated less pronounced abnormalities, and cerebral MRI on hospitalization day 83 (Figure 5C) revealed no significant abnormalities. These findings indicated an improved patient condition and he was successfully discharged on hospitalization day 91.
After discharge, oral steroids combined with tacrolimus were continued, along with monthly maintenance IVIG at a dose of 2 g/kg. In March 2024 (20 months into the disease course), the steroid dosage had been decreased to 2.5 mg/day and assessments showed a CMAS score of 52, complete resolution of the rash (Figure 4B), no neurological symptoms, and normal muscle enzyme levels. There was also a decrease in NXP2 antibody titer IgG to 15.85 RU/ml.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 11-year-old boy presented in July 2022 with a 1-month history of proximal muscle weakness and a heliotrope rash, and two weeks after initiating intensive immunosuppressive therapy developed progressive dysphagia and status epilepticus.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted in July 2022 with 1 month of proximal muscle weakness (Childhood Myositis Assessment Scale [CMAS] score 12) and a classic heliotrope rash. Workup confirmed anti-NXP2-positive juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM; 2017 EULAR/ACR score 14.9), and he was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 g/kg), pulse intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP 500 mg/day for 3 days) followed by oral prednisone (2 mg/kg/day), and intravenous cyclophosphamide (IVCY 500 mg). Despite therapy, muscle weakness persisted and he developed progressive dysphagia. Two weeks into treatment, he suddenly developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures with interictal coma (status epilepticus), requiring endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and emergency PICU admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe anti-NXP2 and anti-Ro-52 antibody-positive juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) diagnosed in July 2022.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, progressive dysphagia, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and skin/periorbital edema; negative for fever during the PICU macrophage activation syndrome evaluation.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: Proximal muscle weakness (CMAS score 12) and typical heliotrope rash. PICU admission (2 weeks post-initial therapy): Comatose between generalized tonic-clonic seizures (status epilepticus), intubated; significant generalized skin and periorbital edema; blood pressure 126/81 mmHg; normal cardiac and pulmonary auscultation; no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly; bilateral positive Babinski signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission labs and diagnostics: Serum creatine kinase (CK) 4,718 U/L (reference: 0–164 U/L), ANA 1:320 (+), anti-NXP2 IgG 115.42 RU/mL, anti-Ro-52 positive; electromyography (EMG) showed myogenic damage; muscle biopsy showed perifascicular atrophy, perivascular/endomysial inflammation, and diffuse sarcolemmal MHC-I positivity. PICU admission labs: AST 269 U/L, ALT 76 U/L, LDH 1,200 U/L, CK 4,784 U/L (later peaking at 16,219 U/L), WBC 17.15 x 10^9/L (91.4% neutrophils), hemoglobin 137 g/L, platelets decreased to 39 x 10^9/L, normal CRP, serum ferritin >2,000 ng/mL, triglycerides 2.56 mmol/L, normal electrolytes and coagulation, and rising anti-NXP2 IgG titer (139.76 RU/mL). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): Normal cell count and glucose, mildly elevated protein (64 mg/dL, reference: 15–45 mg/dL), negative bacterial/viral studies. Echocardiography: Normal cardiac function.
objective.advanced_workup: PICU neuroimaging and EEG: Head CT showed blurred gray-white matter differentiation; contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed abnormal signals in the left parieto-occipital lobe and thalamus (MRA/MRV normal); EEG showed diffuse 2–5 Hz slow-wave background. PICU chest CT: Bilateral lung infiltrates and partial consolidation. PICU day 6 bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Detected Pneumocystis jirovecii. Bone marrow aspirate: Demonstrated hemophagocytic macrophages consistent with macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Active severe anti-NXP2-positive juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) complicated by central nervous system (CNS) involvement (status epilepticus), macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), and opportunistic Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed by BALF mNGS on PICU day 6 and bilateral lung infiltrates/consolidation on chest CT). Plan and clinical course: Managed in the PICU with endotracheal intubation (later tracheostomy for prolonged ventilation), anticonvulsants, four sessions of therapeutic plasma exchange (including two double-filtration plasmapheresis sessions), two additional 3-day pulses of IV methylprednisolone (500 mg/day) followed by maintenance IVMP (1.6 mg/kg/day), monthly IVIG (2 g/kg), oral tacrolimus (FK506) for MAS, and targeted anti-Pneumocystis antifungal/antimicrobial therapy. His seizures resolved, CK normalized to 41 U/L, swallowing and respiratory function recovered allowing ventilator weaning, and brain MRI/EEG abnormalities resolved by day 83, leading to hospital discharge on day 91. At 20-month follow-up (March 2024) on low-dose oral prednisone (2.5 mg/day), tacrolimus, and monthly IVIG, he had complete rash resolution, normal muscle strength (CMAS 52), normal muscle enzymes, and a low anti-NXP2 IgG titer (15.85 RU/mL).
